name: Neonatal hypoglycaemia
aliases: low blood glucose in the newborn

clinicalPearls: A low blood glucose in the newborn period that is common, often transient, but potentially harmful to the developing brain
At-risk groups include infants of diabetic mothers, small- or large-for-gestational-age babies, preterm infants and those who are unwell or cold
It is frequently asymptomatic but can cause jitteriness, poor feeding, hypotonia, apnoea, seizures or a reduced conscious level
Screening of at-risk and symptomatic babies with reliable glucose measurement guides management
Persistent or severe hypoglycaemia beyond the transitional period suggests hyperinsulinism or a metabolic or endocrine disorder
Management ranges from supported feeding to intravenous dextrose, with investigation of refractory cases during a hypoglycaemic episode
reference.pathophysiology: After birth the newborn must transition from a continuous placental glucose supply to intermittent enteral feeding, mobilising glycogen and generating glucose through gluconeogenesis and using alternative fuels such as ketones. Hypoglycaemia arises when demand exceeds supply or counter-regulation is inadequate, for example with limited glycogen stores in growth-restricted or preterm babies, or with excess insulin in infants of diabetic mothers and in congenital hyperinsulinism. Because the brain depends on glucose, prolonged or severe hypoglycaemia, particularly when alternative fuels are lacking, risks neuronal injury.
additionalDifferentials: Transitional hypoglycaemia of the healthy newborn
Endocrine disorders (for example hypopituitarism, cortisol deficiency)
additionalInvestigations: Reliable blood glucose measurement (laboratory-confirmed for low readings)
A hypoglycaemia screen taken during a low-glucose episode in persistent cases
Assessment for sepsis and other acute illness
Metabolic and endocrine investigations for refractory or persistent disease
Monitoring of feeding and glucose response
redFlags: Persistent or recurrent hypoglycaemia beyond the transitional period
Very low glucose requiring high dextrose delivery, suggesting hyperinsulinism
Features suggesting sepsis or a metabolic disorder
reference.prognosis: Transient hypoglycaemia corrected promptly usually has an excellent outcome, but severe, prolonged or recurrent hypoglycaemia, especially with symptoms, carries a risk of neurodevelopmental injury.
pitfalls: Relying on point-of-care meters that are inaccurate at low values
Failing to obtain a hypoglycaemia screen during the episode in persistent cases
Missing hyperinsulinism as a cause of high glucose requirement
Overlooking sepsis or a metabolic disorder
references: British Association of Perinatal Medicine guidance
management: Establish early and frequent enteral feeding as the first-line measure in at-risk infants
Give intravenous dextrose for symptomatic infants or those failing to maintain glucose on feeds, titrating to the glucose response
Treat suspected congenital hyperinsulinism with diazoxide, adding octreotide or glucagon for diazoxide-unresponsive disease
Maintain normothermia and treat concurrent illness such as sepsis that increases glucose demand
Monitor blood glucose with laboratory confirmation of low bedside readings
Take a hypoglycaemia screen during a documented low-glucose episode and investigate persistent disease for metabolic and endocrine disorders
Refer to paediatric endocrine or metabolic services for persistent hyperinsulinism or an inborn error of metabolism
